newsitem.title: USA: Collins and ex-publisher in out-of-court settlement.
newsitem.headline: Collins and ex-publisher in out-of-court settlement.

text.p: British actress Joan Collins has once again beaten the critics.
Collins had the last laugh on Wednesday on a New York publisher that sued her on the grounds that she could not write and it therefore wanted back the $1.2 million advance it paid her for a novel.

Collins and Random House announced they had reached a settlement in a legal battle that seemed headed for the appeals courts after a Manhattan jury ruled last year she could keep the advance, even though the book was bad.
Both sides said Random agreed to pay Collins an undisclosed sum and agreed as well never to reveal the details of the agreement.

Donald Zakarin, lawyer for the 63-year-old actress best known as the scheming Alexis Carrington on "Dynasty," said she was very happy. "The second volume of her autobiography will soon be out in the United States with a chapter on this," he said.
He was referring to the headline-grabbing February 1996 Manhattan trial in which a jury ruled Collins did not have to give Random House its advance back.
Random argued that since the book was incoherent, redundant, sloppy, poorly written and awful, it could not be published and therefore the contract was null and void.
The jury deliberated for 90 minutes and declared quality did not count and that she had, in fact, turned in a completed manuscript.
"A good editor can virtually take the phone book and turn it into something reasonable," said one juror.

A statement from Random House said all appeals in the case were dropped and added, "Both Random House and Joan Collins regret that this matter took the course it did and that it was not resolved sooner and without having to go to court."
